To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the gender pay gap in Germany is at least one‐fifth higher than in the absence of monopsony and that this effect is mainly due to women’s lower labor supply to the monopsonistic firm.
women’s labor market participation is less elastic than that of men and that women’s wages are lower than men’s, even after controlling for observable characteristics.

(i) labor supply elasticities to firms in Germany are very small, and (ii) the labor supply elasticity of women is smaller than the labor supply elasticity men, which is opposite to the gender differences in labor market elasticities usually found in the literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the gender pay gap, labor supply to the employer, and the role of monopsony.
the question of whether the gender pay gap can be attributed to differences between women and men in the degree to which they are willing to work for the same firm.
the question of whether women’s and men's labor supply to firms is elastic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gender pay gap is not only a result of gender discrimination at the market level, but also of gender discrimination at firm level.
monopsony in the labor market is an important determinant of the gender pay difference, and that the pay gap is larger than it would be without monopsony.
monopsonistic labor markets are a plausible explanation for a significant part of the gender pay difference in Germany.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gender wage gap is a result of both the market and the firm.
monopsony is not only a theoretical possibility but also a real-world phenomenon.
the gender pay gap is a result of the combination of gender differences in market labor supply and gender differences in labor demand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
labor supply to monopsonistic firms might be an important factor for the gender pay gap, which has been neglected by the literature so far.
the gender pay gap is likely to be larger in industries with higher monopsony power.
gender differences in labor market outcomes can be explained in part by the fact that women and men respond differently to the incentives provided by the labor market.
